newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK FARMERS TRY TO EVADE POLICE, BLOCK ROADS.
newsitem.headline: GREEK FARMERS TRY TO EVADE POLICE, BLOCK ROADS.

text.p: Greece's defiant farmers drove their tractors through farmland on Tuesday in an effort to evade heavy police forces and cut off highways in this central Thessally region.

Convoys of hundreds of tractors were turned back by police guarding several key road junctions but the farmers continued to try to sneak through the road blocks, tracking through vast cotton fields, eyewitnesses said.
The government successfully waited out a crippling 25-day farmers' road blockade in December, which virtually cut the country in two, but has now vowed to keep roads free.
"We have every legal right to take measures to preserve normalcy. We want to prevent a road blockade," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters.
The government threatened to use force if necessary to thwart a new attempt to block roads. The farmers vowed to continue with their plans but announced they would not clash with police.
About 5,000 police, many in riot gear, and helicopters were dispatched to the area to prevent the farmers from taking over the roads for a second time.
"Terrorism does not work on farmers. Their problems are so deep that all the helicopters and police will not hinder them," farmers' representative Vangelis Boutas told reporters.

Several convoys of hundreds of tractors played a game of hide-and-seek with police, drawing them into farm fields and getting them stuck away from their guarding points in an effort to reach the highways.
"Can you believe it? They sent riot squads to our little village. All we want to do is protest," a farmer driving his tractor in a long convoy shouted at reporters.

The farmers had given up the December blockade because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to highways if their demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel and tax cuts were not met.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis has turned down most of their demands, saying the state budget could not afford to spend an extra drachma on any specific group.
He said his strict 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, along with tight new incomes and tax policies, were necessary to turn the ailing economy around.
